text: At dawn on the seventh of June, 1944, a day after the first Allied troops landed in Normandy, one hundred and fifty ocean tugs appeared on the horizon of the English Channel. Behind them, straining on steel hawsers at barely four knots, crept rows of hollow concrete blocks six stories high, floating steel bridges half a mile long, and fifty-five stripped steamships rigged with charges. Germany's high command believed the invasion of Western Europe would stand or fall on one hard rule of supply. Two Allied armies in France needed at least twelve thousand tons of fuel, ammunition, and rations every day, plus two thousand five hundred vehicles just to stay in the fight. Yet every deepwater port from Cherbourg to Antwerp was ringed with bunkers and wired for demolition. Instead of storming a French port head-on, British and American engineers built two artificial harbors the size of Dover in secret across Britain, sank the pieces underwater to hide them from German reconnaissance aircraft, and towed one point five million tons of concrete and steel across one hundred miles of mined sea. The blueprint for those floating ports was written in blood on nineteenth of August 1942 on the pebble beaches of Dieppe. Operation Jubilee was mounted by combined operations under Vice Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten to test whether an amphibious force could seize and hold a defended Channel port by direct assault. Just over six thousand and eighty-six men embarked from England, nearly five thousand of them from the Second Canadian Infantry Division, backed by twenty-nine Churchill tanks. Within three hours, the raid was a catastrophe. Dieppe sat between two steep chalk headlands hollowed out with German gun casemates. On the main beach, loose flint cobbles called churchingle jammed the tracks of the Churchill tanks, while a six-foot sea wall blocked the way into town. Every tank landed on the beach was lost or trapped. By midday, when the surviving craft pulled back, three thousand six hundred and twenty-three men had been killed, wounded, or captured, almost sixty percent of the force. When Lieutenant General Frederick Morgan set up the COSSAC planning staff in London in spring 1943 to draft Operation Overlord, the lesson of Dieppe sat on every desk. Across northern France, German engineers had turned Cherbourg, Le Havre, Boulogne, Calais, and Dunkirk into fortresses with demolition charges packed inside the lock gates, cranes, and key walls. Even if Allied troops surrounded a major port from inland, German engineers would blow the keys and scuttle ships across the entrance before surrendering. History proved Morgan right. When US troops took Cherbourg on the twenty-seventh of June 1944, three weeks after D-Day, the harbor was so wrecked and mined that it could not handle cargo in bulk until August. If the Allies could not take a port, they had to land across open beaches in the Bay of the Seine. Yet open beaches posed a severe mechanical problem. Along the Normandy coast, the Channel tide rises and falls by up to twenty-four feet at spring tides, the height of a two-story house. Because the beaches slope so gently, as the tide ebbs, the waterline retreats up to half a mile out to sea twice a day. A flat-bottomed tank landing ship, or LST, could beach near high water, wait for the tide to drop, and drive its vehicles onto sand. But she was then stranded for ten to twelve hours until the next high tide floated her off. Deep-draft Liberty ships carrying ten thousand tons of shells, steel, and fuel drums had to anchor two miles offshore and swing every crate into barges or six-wheel DUKW amphibious trucks rocking in open swells. One northeasterly gale would halt beach unloading and leave the armies ashore short of ammunition while German panzers counterattacked. The seed of the solution had been planted before Dieppe. On thirtieth of May 1942, Prime Minister Winston Churchill dictated a one-page minute to Mountbatten titled "Piers for Use on Beaches." Having watched supply barges ground on tidal flats in the First World War, Churchill refused to let the invasion of France stall on the same obstacle. His directive was forty-eight words long. "They must float up and down with the tide," Churchill wrote. "The anchor problem must be mastered. Let me have the best solution worked out. Don't argue the matter. The difficulties will argue for themselves." Turning those words into steel fell to the Directorate of Transportation at the War Office, led by Brigadier, later Major General, Sir Bruce White. By early 1943, three rival designs competed. The first came from Hugh Iris Hughes, a Welsh civil engineer in London, who proposed towing concrete pier heads, codenamed Hippos, across the Channel and sinking them in thirty feet of water, linked to shore by rigid steel lattice bridges called Crocodiles. The second design came from a twenty-nine-year-old civil engineer named Alan Beckett, working under Bruce White. Beckett argued that any rigid bridge in the Channel would wrench itself apart when a wave lifted one pontoon while the next dropped into a trough. Instead, Beckett designed a floating steel roadway, codenamed Whale, built in eighty-foot spans resting on pontoons called Beetles. Crucially, Beckett left the center of each eighty-foot span open so the side girders could twist like a torsion bar. Where standard bridges locked rigid, a whale span could twist by up to forty degrees along its length without bending a single member, riding diagonal swells like a snake's spine. At the seaward end stood a floating steel pier head called a Spud pontoon, two hundred feet by sixty feet on four eighty-nine-foot steel legs. Diesel electric winches let the deck slide up and down its legs as the twenty-four-foot tide rose and fell while ships berthed alongside. A third engineer, Commander Robert Lockner of the Admiralty, tackled the outer sea wall. Knowing that most wave energy sits in the top ten feet of water, Lockner designed the Bombardon, a two-hundred-foot floating steel cross, twenty-five feet high, with its lower arm flooded for pendulum inertia. Moored in double rows offshore, Bombardons were built to cut an eight-foot channel wave in half. To test all three in secret, the War Office built an experimental port at Garleston on Wigtown Bay in southwest Scotland, matching Normandy's twenty-four-foot tides, wide mudflats, and gales. Through summer 1943, troops and engineers erected full-scale prototypes of Hughes' fixed Hippos and Beckett's floating Whale roadway side by side in the surf. In August 1943, a summer gale roared up the Solway Firth and gave the verdict. Heavy surf scoured the sand from under Hughes' fixed Hippos, tilting the piers and wrenching the Crocodile spans off their bearings. Right beside them, Beckett's flexible Whale roadway rode and twisted with the waves undamaged. The storm also proved Beckett's kite anchor. Shaped like an underwater box kite, its fluke dug deeper into the sand the harder a wave pulled, holding thirty tons of tension where three-ton anchors dragged through. While that gale blew, Mountbatten and Bruce White sailed to Canada aboard the Queen Mary with Churchill for the Quebec Conference. On twenty-fourth of August 1943, Churchill, President Franklin Roosevelt, and the combined chiefs approved two portable ports, Mulberry A for the US First Army at Omaha Beach and Mulberry B for the British Second Army at Arromanches on Gold Beach. D-Day was nine months away, and not a single caisson had been poured. A Mulberry harbor had five interlocking rings. Furthest offshore, in eleven to fifteen fathoms of water, floated two lines of steel Bombardons. One thousand yards closer in sat the main spine, a curved wall of giant hollow concrete boxes called Phoenix caissons, sunk nose to tail on the seabed. Flanking the concrete wall in shallower water lay lines of scuttled ships called Gooseberries. Inside that two-square-mile sheltered basin stood the floating Spud pier heads, linked to the beach by half-mile Whale roadways. In September 1943, the Ministry of Supply and the War Office ordered civil engineering contractors to build the Phoenix caissons, Spud piers, and ten miles of Whale bridging before May 1944. One hundred and forty-seven reinforced concrete Phoenix caissons for the June assault, plus sixty-five supplementary units that summer. Two hundred and twelve concrete giants in all. The largest, the Type A1 caisson, measured two hundred and four feet long, fifty-six feet three inches wide, and sixty feet high, as tall as a six-story building and two-thirds the length of a football pitch. Each A1 caisson displaced six thousand and forty-four tons, carried crew quarters, a forty-millimeter Bofors gun tower, and twenty-two internal flooding chambers controlled by Kingston valves. Immediately, the build hit a bottleneck. British dry docks were packed with warships and Atlantic freighters, leaving room for fewer than a third of the caissons. Sir Malcolm McAlpine and John Mowlem, engineers, proposed a bold workaround along the muddy banks of the Thames at Rotherhithe, Deptford, Erith, and Barking. Steam excavators dug twelve vast earthen basins straight into the clay banks beside the Thames, leaving an earth levee holding back the river. In those mud pits, gangs worked round the clock under blackout lamps to pour the bottom fifteen feet of the holes. Once cured, bulldozers breached the earth bank at high tide, flooding the pit. Tugs towed the floating concrete trays into wet commercial docks, such as the East and South West India docks, where gangs poured the upper forty-five feet of walls while the caissons floated. Across Britain, forty-five thousand workers from over three hundred firms were mobilized. In seven winter months, they poured six hundred thousand cubic yards, one point two million tons of concrete, laced with thirty-one thousand tons of steel bar and framed in fifteen million square feet of shuttering timber, while steelworks from Glasgow to South Wales fabricated the whale spans and spud pontoons. By April 1944, a new question arose: Where to hide one hundred and forty-seven six-story concrete blocks along the south coast without German reconnaissance pilots spotting them? Rear Admiral William Tennant, who had organized the Dunkirk evacuation and now commanded the British Mulberry force, ordered them hidden under the sea. Each night, tugs towed finished Phoenix units to sandbanks off Selsey Bill in Sussex and Dungeness in Kent, opened the valves, and sank them in thirty feet of water. From forty thousand feet, rare Luftwaffe reconnaissance flights saw only low rims above the surf, dismissing them as barges or sea walls. Berlin never suspected two ports were sitting on the Channel floor. Three days before D-Day, the resurrection began. Royal Navy and US Navy salvage vessels pulled alongside the submerged parks at Selsey and Dungeness, coupled suction hoses, and pumped thousands of tons of water out of the holes. One by one, crusted in weed, the six-thousand-ton concrete boxes broke free of the mud and rose forty feet into the air. Towing them to Normandy took every spare tug the Allies could muster. One hundred and fifty tugs from fifteen hundred horsepower American diesel electric salvage tugs and Dutch ocean tugs like the Zwarte Zee to Clyde Harbor tugs. Because a flat-ended caisson had the drag of a house brick, two heavy tugs pulling on one-thousand-foot wire horses hauled each A1 caisson across one hundred miles of swept minefield lanes at barely four knots, a brisk walking pace. Even harder to tow were the whale roadways, linked in four hundred and eighty foot strings of six spans on their beetle pontoons. In the six-foot chop of mid-Channel, waves washed over the small concrete beetles. If a hatch leaked or a cable snatched, the lead pontoon dived under the swell, dragging the span with it. Nearly forty percent of the initial whale tows bound for Omaha suffered flooded pontoons or parted cables on the crossing. First to arrive off the beaches on 7th June, D plus one, were the fifty-five elderly ships of the Gooseberry Squadrons, code-named Corncobs. Worn-out merchantmen joined by four old warships, including the British pre-dreadnought HMS Centurion, the Dutch cruiser Sumatra, and the French battleship Corbe. Their volunteer crews steamed into five shallow arcs off Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword Beaches, anchored nose to tail, and fired scuttling charges in the holds. Within forty-eight hours, fifty-five hulls displacing three hundred and twenty thousand tons rested on the sand in thirteen to fifteen feet of water, their upper decks standing dry above the surf to shelter small craft. On 8th and 9th June, the first Phoenix caissons reached Omaha Beach under US Navy Captain Augustine Gray, and Arromanches under Rear Admiral Tennant. Planting a six thousand and forty-four ton block in a three knot current took stopwatch precision. As two tugs held the bow and a third nudged the stern into line with surveyors transits on shore, twelve ratings on the high catwalk spun the Kingston flood valves. With a roar of escaping air, seawater flooded the twenty-two chambers. Sixteen to twenty-two minutes later, six thousand tons of concrete settled onto the seabed, leaving twenty feet of wall above the highest spring tide. Unit by unit, the two outer breakwaters grew across the bay until each harbor enclosed two square miles of calm water. Inside the walls, Seabees at Omaha and Royal Engineers at Arromanches worked eighteen-hour shifts, winching the eighty-nine foot legs of the spud pier heads down to the seabed and bolting together the half-mile whale roadways to shore. By 16th June, ten days after D-Day, both floating ports were open. At Omaha, an LST nosed into the pier head and rolled 78 loaded trucks down the floating bridge onto French soil in 38 minutes, a job that had taken 12 hours on drying sand. That same day at Arromanches, the 1,500-ton coaster SS Cormount berthed at the pier head and unloaded shells straight onto lorries. 48 hours later, the barometer plunged. At dawn on 19th of June, 1944, D plus 13, a fierce northeasterly gale of force six to force eight swept down the Channel, gusting to 45 knots. Weather logs showed no June storm like it had hit Normandy in 40 years. Worse, the gale struck at the peak of the spring tides, driving waves 12 to 15 feet high into the Bay of the Seine for four days and nights. The 96-hour storm exposed a decisive geographical and engineering difference between the American harbor at Omaha and the British harbor 12 miles east at Arromanches. At Arromanches, Mulberry B sat behind a submerged limestone ridge called the Calvados Reef, a mile offshore, which tripped the biggest deep-water rollers before they hit the wall. At Omaha, Mulberry A had no offshore reef. Its caissons stood in deeper water, exposed to 100 miles of open sea. The collapse at Omaha started half a mile outside the concrete wall along the double line of moored bombardons. Built for eight-foot waves and force six winds, their wire moorings endured seven times their design stress under 15-foot storm waves. One after another, the cables parted. Driven by 40 knot winds and spring tides, 25 runaway bombardons, each a 1,500 ton steel ram 200 feet long, drifted into Mulberry A. Inside the harbor, those loose floats battered the Whale roadways in the Phoenix wall, joined by over 100 landing craft and Rhino ferries that dragged their anchors into the bridges. At the same time, the concrete wall failed from below. In the rush to finish Mulberry A, several Phoenix caissons at Omaha had been sunk onto uneven sand without anti-scour mattresses or sand ballast inside their chambers. As 15-foot waves poured over the unballasted boxes, the undertow sucked away the sand beneath their ends. Unsupported at bow and stern, 6,000-ton caissons cracked down the middle under their own weight and split open. Within 24 hours, 20 of the 31 Phoenix caissons in Mulberry A's outer wall had broken apart, letting the full channel surf tear the western Whale bridges to pieces. 12 miles east at Arromanches, Mulberry B took a hard pounding, too. Six Phoenix caissons cracked or shifted, and several bombardons broke adrift. Yet behind the Calvados Reef, and because Bruce White's engineers had leveled the seabed and pumped thousands of tons of sand inside the hollow Phoenix chambers to weight them down, the main wall at Arromanches held. Even at the height of the gale on 20th of June, British lorries at Arromanches rolled down the twisting Whale roadways with 800 tons of ammunition and stores. When the wind dropped on 22nd of June, over 300 Allied landing craft lay stranded along the beaches, and Mulberry A was a ruin of broken concrete and twisted steel. Lieutenant General Omar Bradley, commanding the US First Army, inspected the wreckage with Rear Admiral John Hall and Captain Edward Elsberg and made a pragmatic call. Rather than spend weeks rebuilding Mulberry A's outer wall, Bradley ordered the deepwater piers at Omaha abandoned. US engineers reinforced the inner Gooseberry block ship line at Omaha with supplementary caissons and turned the lagoon into a beaching basin for LSTs and DUKWs. Every intact Spud pier head, Whale span, and Beetle pontoon salvaged from Omaha was towed 12 miles east to Arromanches, turning British Mulberry B into one heavily reinforced port for the beachhead. Through July and August 1944, as Allied armies broke out of Normandy toward the Seine, Arromanches, christened Port Winston, became one of the busiest harbors on Earth. Using salvaged US spans and 65 newly poured reinforced Phoenix caissons towed from the Thames, Royal Engineers doubled the northern wall, packed the caissons with half a million tons of sand ballast, and expanded the floating Whale roadways until seven miles of bridgework spanned the bay. Solid cargo over the piers at Arromanches and the beaches at Omaha were soon joined by a second fleet under the seabed. Armored divisions racing across France burned hundreds of thousands of gallons of petrol a day. In 1942, Arthur Hartley, chief engineer of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, had worked with Mountbatten's staff to create Operation Pluto, Pipelines under the Ocean. Hartley's team built two types of undersea fuel pipe. The first, HAIS cable, used submarine telegraph machinery at Siemens Brothers on the Thames to wrap a three-inch lead pipe in steel tape and wire to hold 1,500 pounds per square inch of pressure. The second, Hamel pipe, wound 70 miles of welded three-inch steel tubing around floating steel drums forty feet high and sixty feet wide, each displacing sixteen hundred tons and named HMS Conundrum. Towed behind tugs, a conundrum spool rotated in the water and laid continuous steel pipe onto the channel floor. After the initial seventy-mile Bambi Route from the Isle of Wight to Cherbourg suffered anchor and rock damage in August 1944, the shorter thirty-mile Dumbo lines laid from Dungeness to Boulogne that autumn succeeded. Seventeen undersea pipelines pumped from camouflaged stations inside English seaside bungalows eventually delivered over one million gallons of petrol a day, one hundred and seventy-two million imperial gallons in total before VE Day. After the war, historians asked a sharp question. Since US crews at Omaha and Utah landed ten thousand to fifteen thousand tons a day directly over the open sand using beached LSTs and DUKWs once the June storm passed, were the Mulberry harbors worth their cost? The official logistics tables compiled by SHAEF and US Army historian Roland Ruppenthal give a clear answer. Open beaches handled bulk vehicles and rations rapidly in calm summer weather, but they could not lift heavy locomotives, bridging girders, or crated shells without cranes, nor could they work when autumn gales shut the surf zone. At Arromanches, Mulberry B beat its own design target. Built for six thousand tons a day, Port Winston averaged six thousand seven hundred and sixty-five tons a day through July 1944 and peaked at over nine thousand tons in a single day. More importantly, Mulberry B was the Allied army's insurance against the calendar. German demolitions and resistance on the Scheldt estuary kept the giant port of Antwerp closed until the twenty-eighth of November 1944, nearly six months after D-Day. Designed for ninety days of summer use, the concrete caissons and flexing whale bridges of Arromanches stayed in service for five full months into the November gales. By the time Mulberry B closed at the end of November 1944, the Normandy beachhead and its artificial port at Arromanches had landed over two point five million men, five hundred thousand vehicles, and four million tons of supplies, including five hundred and twenty thousand tons of direct pier and coaster cargo and two hundred and twenty thousand troops across Arromanches' own floating roadways. Those two hundred and twelve hollow concrete boxes had broken the central premise of Germany's Atlantic Wall. By proving that an industrial nation could build a deepwater port in its own rivers and tow it across the sea, Britain and the United States showed that an invading army no longer had to capture a harbor to liberate Europe. They brought their harbor with them.
